questions.q: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=e^x$, using $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2!}x^2+\dfrac{f'''(0)}{3!}x^3+\cdots$.
questions.answer: Since every derivative of $e^x$ equals $e^x$, and $e^0=1$: all derivatives at $0$ equal $1$. So $e^x\approx1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}+\dfrac{x^3}{3!}=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}$.

sections.heading: Using known series to build new ones

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series for $e^x$, find the Maclaurin series for $e^{-2x}$ up to the term in $x^3$.

Given the Maclaurin series $\sin x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}$ and $\cos x\approx1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}$, find the Maclaurin series for $\tan x$ up to the term in $x^3$, using $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and polynomial division.

sections.heading: Using a Maclaurin series to approximate a value

questions.q: Use the Maclaurin series for $e^x$ up to the $x^3$ term to approximate $e^{0.1}$, to four decimal places, and compare with the true value $e^{0.1}\approx1.10517$.
questions.answer: $e^{0.1}\approx1+0.1+\dfrac{(0.1)^2}{2}+\dfrac{(0.1)^3}{6}=1+0.1+0.005+0.0001\overline{6}\approx1.1052$. This is very close to the true value $1.10517$, with an error of about $0.00003$.

sections.heading: Tests for convergence of a series

questions.q: Use the ratio test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{n}{2^n}$ converges.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{(n+1)/2^{n+1}}{n/2^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n+1}{2n}=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $\dfrac{1}{2}<1$, the series converges.

questions.q: Use the ratio test to determine whether the Maclaurin series for $e^x$, $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{n!}$, converges for all real $x$.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\dfrac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{x^n/n!}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{|x|}{n+1}=0$ for any fixed $x$. Since the limit is $0<1$ regardless of $x$, the series converges for all real values of $x$.

questions.q: Use the ratio test to find the radius of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{n}$.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\dfrac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)}{x^n/n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n|x|}{n+1}=|x|$. The series converges when $|x|<1$, so the radius of convergence is $R=1$.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n!\,x^n$, and explain what this tells us about where the series is useful.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\dfrac{(n+1)!\,x^{n+1}}{n!\,x^n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)|x|=\infty$ for any $x\neq0$. Since this limit is never less than $1$ (except at $x=0$), the radius of convergence is $R=0$ — the series only converges at the single point $x=0$, making it useless as an approximation anywhere else.

sections.heading: Comparing a Maclaurin approximation to the exact function

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series $\cos x\approx1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^4}{24}$, approximate $\cos(0.3)$ to four decimal places, and compare with the true value $\cos(0.3)\approx0.9553$.
questions.answer: $\cos(0.3)\approx1-\dfrac{(0.3)^2}{2}+\dfrac{(0.3)^4}{24}=1-0.045+0.0003375\approx0.9553$. This matches the true value to four decimal places, showing the Maclaurin approximation is highly accurate for small $x$.

questions.q: Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$ up to the term in $x^4$, using $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+\dfrac{f''(0)}{2!}x^2+\dfrac{f'''(0)}{3!}x^3+\dfrac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}x^4$.

sections.heading: Determining the interval of convergence using the ratio test

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of the Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+x)$, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}$, using the ratio test.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\dfrac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)}{x^n/n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n|x|}{n+1}=|x|$. The series converges when $|x|<1$, so the radius of convergence is $R=1$ (consistent with the earlier result found for a structurally similar series).

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series $e^x\approx1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{1-x}\approx1+x+x^2$ (valid for small $x$), find the Maclaurin series for $\dfrac{e^x}{1-x}$ up to the term in $x^2$, by multiplying the two series together.
questions.answer: Multiply term by term, keeping only terms up to $x^2$: $\left(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)(1+x+x^2)=1+x+x^2+x+x^2+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+O(x^3)=1+2x+\dfrac{5x^2}{2}+O(x^3)$. So $\dfrac{e^x}{1-x}\approx1+2x+\dfrac{5}{2}x^2$.

sections.heading: Using differentiation to find a Maclaurin series

questions.q: Given the Maclaurin series $\dfrac{1}{1-x}\approx1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ for $|x|<1$, differentiate both sides term by term to find the Maclaurin series for $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}$ up to the term in $x^2$.
questions.answer: Differentiating $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}$ on the left. Differentiating the right side term by term: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots\right)=1+2x+3x^2+\cdots$. So $\dfrac{1}{(1-x)^2}\approx1+2x+3x^2$.

sections.heading: Estimating an error bound in a Maclaurin approximation

questions.q: The Maclaurin series for $\sin x$ truncated after the $x^3$ term is $\sin x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}$. Use this to approximate $\sin(0.2)$ to four decimal places, and find the absolute error compared to the true value $\sin(0.2)\approx0.19867$.
questions.answer: $\sin(0.2)\approx0.2-\dfrac{(0.2)^3}{6}=0.2-\dfrac{0.008}{6}=0.2-0.001333\approx0.19867$. Absolute error: $|0.19867-0.19867|\approx0.00000$ (to four decimal places), showing that even a low-order Maclaurin approximation is extremely accurate for small values of $x$ close to $0$.

questions.q: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=(1+x)^{1/2}$, using the binomial series $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx+\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}x^2$ with $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Use the Maclaurin series for $e^x$ up to the $x^4$ term to approximate $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x-1-x}{x^2}$, and check that your answer matches the value obtained using L'Hopital's rule.
questions.answer: Using $e^x\approx1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots$: $e^x-1-x\approx\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots$. Dividing by $x^2$: $\dfrac{e^x-1-x}{x^2}\approx\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{x}{6}+\cdots$, which tends to $\dfrac{1}{2}$ as $x\to0$. Using L'Hopital's rule twice on the original limit (since it is initially $\frac{0}{0}$) gives $\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x-1}{2x}=\dfrac{e^0}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, confirming the same result.

questions.q: This question has three parts. (a) Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\cos(x^2)$ up to the term in $x^8$, by substituting $x^2$ into the known series $\cos u\approx1-\dfrac{u^2}{2}+\dfrac{u^4}{24}$. (b) Use your result to write down an approximation for $\int_0^1\cos(x^2)\,dx$ as a sum of simple fractions (this integral has no elementary closed form, so series approximation is genuinely useful here). (c) Evaluate this approximation as a single decimal, to three decimal places.
